bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: The Yale Library has been the heart of the university ever since, according to tradition, ten ministers met at the house of Reverend Samuel Russel in Branford in 1701 and contributed 40 books to found Yale College. The books were taken to Killingworth in 1704 where the Rector Abraham Pierson resided and then upon his death in 1707 to Saybrook, the seat of the College, where they remained until 1718. At that time the College was to move to New Haven, but the people of Saybrook forcibly resisted the transfer of books. Many volumes and papers were lost in the scramble.

The Senior Tutor acted as Librarian until 1805 and received an extra five pounds to his yearly salary for sorting and cataloguing the books. The tutor's efforts at book acquisition were aided by several large gifts of books from prominent people such as Jeremiah Drummer, Elihu Yale, and Bishop George Berkeley so that by 1742 when Rector Thomas Clap and Tutor John Worthington compiled the first library catalogue, there were 2,600 volumes. This grew to 4,000 volumes by 1765.

During the Revolution three quarters of the Library's volumes were removed from New Haven for safe keeping from the enemy. Although they were painstakingly reassembled after the war, only 2,448 books had been recovered by 1782. After the war, donations picked up again. There was increasing need for book storage space because of aggressive acquisition on the part of early librarians and faculty members.

The librarians acted as the guiding force in the library's development. Prior to 1805 the Senior Tutor acted as Librarian. Prof. James L. Kingsley was named the first librarian in 1805 and remained in that position until 1824. Prof. J. W. Gibbs succeeded Kingsley until 1843. Edward Herrick served as Librarian from 1843-58 and D. C. Gilman from 1858-65. Gilman's resignation in 1865 brought in Addison Van Name until 1905. John Christopher Schwab was Librarian from 1905-16 and Andrew Keough was Librarian from 1916-38 through the 1930 move to the Sterling Library. The Records of subsequent librarians can be found in Records of the Librarian 1904-to the present.

A series of sites were used by the library after the college moved to New Haven. In 1718 the books were housed in a library on the 2nd floor, south end of the original Yale College building at the corner of College and Chapel Streets. As new buildings were constructed and the old deteriorated, library apace was provided on an upper floor af the First Chapel (Athenaeum) in 1783, in the rhetorical chamber of the Connecticut Lyceum in 1801, and in the attic of the Second Chapel in 1824. It wasn't until 1842 that the first separate library building (now Dwight Chapel) was constructed by architect Henry Austin.

The early library collected primarily in the sciences, classics, theology, English literature, mathematics, and philosophy, and restricted borrowing to the college officers, faculty members of the professional and scientific schools, and Junior and Senior classes. As a result literary society libraries were founded (Linonian 1753, Brothers-in-Unity 1768, Calliopean 1819) to supplement the college library. Their books on languages, modern history, literature and the arts were brought together with the Yale Library books under one roof upon construction of the Old Library. The central nave was used for the Yale Library and the two wings for the society libraries. This brought the aggregate number of books available to the Yale community to 35,000. By 1871 when the society libraries were brought under Yale library control this number had grown to 95,000 volumes and 20,000 pamphlets and expanded to 161,000 by 1884. By 1886 six thousand volumes were being added every year and a new library to house them was planned. In 1887 funds were provided for construction of the Chittenden Library designed by architect J.C. Cady. It was not many years after its completion in 1889 that more space was needed. Linsly Hall was built by architect Charles C. Haight in 1905 to connect the Old Library (Dwight Hall) with the Chittenden Library. As early as 1918 a new library was under discussion. In 1919 the Yale Corporation decided to construct the Sterling Memorial Library as the principal memorial to be erected from the John Sterling bequest. Construction was under the direction of James Gamble Rogers. The massive centrally located collegiate gothic library was built to house three and one half million volumes and allowed them to function truly as the center of the university.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Records of the University Librarian contains the earliest documentation for the University Library. The majority of the records date from 1808 to the construction and subsequent move to the Sterling Library in 1930.

The University Librarian's records document the full range of library activities and development. The records are arranged in four series and subsequent accessions: Series I Librarian's Correspondence and Reports; Series II Public Services; Series III Technical Services; Series IV Business Services.

Series-I, LIBRARIAN'S CORRESPONDENCE AND REPORTS, consists of five boxes of Correspondence, 1730 [1805-44] sent to the various librarians, the Yale College treasurer, and the Yale President relating to library business; an alphabetical card index to the correspondence 1829-86; annual Reports, 1828 [1844-81]; general Reports to the Librarian 1881-1925; and Miscellaneous records. The letters cover the spectrum of library activities and include correspondence with book exporters, invoices, notes, advertisements, numeric lists of book holdings, book orders, donations, miscellaneous catalogues, statistics on reading room attendance, reading room accounts, literary society purchases and expenses, wills, and memoranda. Henry Barnard, Selah Merrill, and Yung Wing are among the correspondents. Annual reports not only document the statistical growth of the library but include donor information, expenses, library building construction, and literary society library activities.

Series II, PUBLIC SERVICES, [1753-l930] 1945, consists of 21 boxes of Circulation and Reference records. These include circulation charges, statistics, missing book lists, user pledges, subject classifications and reserve book lists. Through the voluminous circulation records (1753-1905) one can document patron use of the library and reconstruct the subject interest of individual readers.

Series III, TECHNICAL SERVICES, contains 24 boxes documenting Cataloguing, Acquisitions, and Preparation functions of the library from 1713 [1823-1925]. These include library classification systems, subject catalogues, collection catalogues, general accessions, purchases, orders, wants, and binding records. Volumes of donation lists with date, donor, name of book or description of donated item account for a large portion of series. Accession books included in this series were maintained until 1904-05. After that date the accession record was kept on cards which were subsequently discarded. (The 1742 catalogues by Rector Thomas Clap and Tutor Worthington are housed at the Beinecke Rare Book Library as are records of the earliest donations by Jeremiah Drummer in 1712 and 1718, Daniel Turner c. 1720, Joseph Thompson 1730, Bishop George Berkeley 1733, Elihu Yale, John Pierson and Sir John Davie C. circa 1714-1717. Consult the Beinecke catalogue for individual listings.)

Series IV, BUSINESS SERVICES, 1701 [1797-1904] 1929, contains General Library Expenses which includes invoices and receipts for binding book purchases, subscriptions, architects fees, staff salaries, supplies, library construction, society library purchases, and housekeeping tasks. Other library expenses are documented in Miscellaneous Accounts which include sources for some of the earliest library funds. The Physical Plant subseries contains contracts with architects and contractors.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series I has three subseries: CORRESPONDENCE, 1918-1938, SUBJECT FILE, 1918-1938, and NON-LIBRARY FILE, 1918-1938. Some material in all subseries is dated prior to 1918 or after 1938.

The subseries, CORRESPONDENCE, is arranged alphabetically by name of individual, institution, organization, or subject. Within the folder, material is arranged chronologically. There is correspondence concerning the American Library Association, the American Library Institute, the Carnegie Corporation, Harvard Library, the Library of Congress, Michigan University, the New Haven Colony Historical Society, and the united states. Major correspondents include George Watson Cole, William Fowler Hopson, and William H. Owen.

The subseries, SUBJECT FILE, is arranged alphabetically by subject. Included are reports, publications g forms, notes, newspaper clippings, photographs, and miscellaneous material. Material refers to Yale University Library administrative matters including personnel, individual departments, funds, various collections, loans, the librarian's report for years of 1914-1940, and information on Sterling Memorial Library.

The third subseries NON-LIBRARY FILE, is also arranged alphabetically by subject. Types of materials are reports, memoranda, publications, newspaper clippings, statistical records, and miscellaneous. This material is concerned with Yale activities or groups outside the library, including schools, student organizations, and clubs, traditions, class organizations from 1842-1936, and university administrative matters.

The order of listing items follows the original registry system. Within each individual listing the material is in chronological order. An alphabetical index to this series lists all entries by name of individual, organization, institution, country, or subject matter.

Included in this series is correspondence to and from important individuals, schools, business organizations, professional groups, cultural organizations, libraries, publishers, miscellaneous historical groups, churches, and others. A large amount of material is concerned with different aspects of Yale University.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Contained in this series are library budgets, appropriation ledgers for different colleges and departments, salary reports, and miscellaneous information on financial policies for collections, appointments, retirement funds, and other matters. Types of material include reports, letters, financial records, memoranda, minutes, and printed materials.

Library budgets are arranged chronologically at the beginning of the series. Within each year the material is in the order of preliminary draft, final budget, and then miscellaneous information. Budgets are followed by appropriation ledgers in alphabetical order by department title, and chronological arrangements of budget figures, salaries, and treasurer's reports on salaries.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series contains three subseries: CORRESPONDENCE, SUBJECT FILE, and NON-LIBRARY FILE. Most of this material dates from 1965 to 1968, although a substantial amount starts at least from 1960, with some items ranging from 1940 to 1968 inclusively, some from 1969, and a few not dated.

CORRESPONDENCE is arranged alphabetically by name of individual, organization, institution, or subject. Folders with continuous topics are arranged chronologically. The subseries contains records pertaining to various programs, departments, collections, committees, funds and contributors, and matters of library administration.

In the SUBJECT FILE miscellaneous material is found at the beginning of each letter of the alphabet, and all items are arranged alphabetically continuous subjects are grouped and arranged chronologically. The subseries contains memoranda, minutes, material pertaining, to committees, collections, funds, several library associations, colleges and universities, Medical Library, Paul Mellon, Research and Development, Vinland Map, and items in connection with many individuals, as well as administration.

The NON-LIBRARY FILE is arranged alphabetically by subject. Prominent records are those related to alumni, school and departmental libraries, councils on Studies, Kline Science Library, Medical Library, Press, and administrative matters.
